detail.longDescription: I want to write a SupportsPut protocol that defines an abstract method named put . It should allow multiprocessing.Queue.put and queue.Queue.put of the standard library as valid implementations. However, looking at the source, they have an argument name mismatch ( obj vs. item ): # in multiprocessing.Queue: def put(self, obj, block=True, timeout=None): ... # in queue.Queue: def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... So if I try to make them both SupportsPut s, I can only choose either obj or item as the protocol method argument: class SupportsPut(Protocol): def put(self, item, block=True, timeout=None): ... If I test it: def do_something_with(thing: SupportsPut): thing.put("hello") do_something_with(mp.Queue()) # <- do_something_with(q.Queue()) I get as expected a Pylance error that mp.Queue.put doesn’t conform to the protocol’s put . In the snippet, do_something_with() treats the first argument positionally, by calling .put("hello") instead of .put(obj="hello") or put(item="hello") , thus avoiding the name conflict. However, SupportsPut.put must choose one of the two names. Is allowing both signatures proper duck typing? If the protocol were @runtime_checkable , what would it make sense for isinstance(mp.Queue(), SupportsPut) to return? How should I write the Protocol so that both Pylance and isinstance() are satisfied? This argument name mismatch is just one example of accounting for slight variations in implementation signatures. In most cases the variation can be resolved by sticking to what fits both, as shown above. Examples: # two implementations: def foo(self, val: Any): ... def foo(self, val: int): ... # can be resolved by passing only an int: thing_that_supports_foo.foo(42) def foo(self, **kwargs): ... def foo(self): ... # can be resolved by not passing extra kwargs: thing_that_supports_foo.foo() Is there a general method of writing a Protocol for these situations?
